p.title: A Network-Based Measure of Cosponsorship Influence on Bill Passing in the United States House of Representatives

ext.title: A Network-Based Measure of Cosponsorship Influence on Bill Passage in the United States House of Representatives
ext.year: 2024 (arXiv v1, June 2024; this file is v2, revised 23 Nov 2025)
ext.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.19554v2 [cs.SI]. Metadata hint confirmed: title, authors, arXiv ID all match the PDF header.
ext.document_type: arXiv preprint; empirical political network analysis (no peer-review status stated in text)
ext.coverage: Read in full: _text/139df50e52fc.txt lines 1-970 (printed pp. 1-26, through the full reference list). Annotation JSON read in full: 44 markup items, all pages 2-26. Figures 1-7 are present only as captions and axis labels in the extracted text, so plotted values are not available; figure-based numbers below come from the text. The text file ends at printed p. 26; no content was skipped.
ext.research_question: Does a legislator-influence measure built from House bill cosponsorship, where two members accrue influence when a bill they both cosponsor passes and that influence decays over time, help explain which House bills pass? Does it beat conventional centralities (eigenvector, closeness, strength) as a signal of bill passage? (Sec. 1, pp. 1-2; Sec. 4-5, pp. 5-18)
ext.theory: Influence accrues between legislators through repeated mutual cosponsorship of bills that pass (quid pro quo / logrolling, social capital, homophily, alliance formation; pp. 3-4). Influence capital accumulates with tenure and decays when a member is inactive (p. 7). Bill-level influence is meant to capture the 'influentials' idea that a few very influential people drive opinion and decisions (p. 13, citing Weimann [49] and Watts and Dodds [51]).
ext.data: US House of Representatives bills, 111th-115th Congresses (Jan 2009 to Jan 2019), from ProPublica bulk bill data (ref [39]). Member IDs completed from Congress Legislators, Stewart and Woon, and McCrain data (refs [40-42]). Only bills are kept; simple, concurrent and joint resolutions are excluded (p. 4). Passage means success through introduction, committee and debate stages in the House, irrespective of Senate or enactment (p. 5). Units: bill (bill-level influence scores), legislator-month (influence I[t,i]), and legislator-pair-month (C tensors). N is not reported as a total bill count or member count anywhere in the text; only percentages appear. Table 1 (p. 7): share of House-originated bills passing in the House, Congresses 111-115: 10.98%, 7.3%, 9.8%, 11.84%, 13.49%. Share enacted into law: 3.87%, 2.96%, 3.55%, 3.31%, 3.84%. Mean cosponsors per bill: 21.50, 21.44, 21.96, 20.93, 19.01 (max 419, 425, 379, 332, 381). Mean bills per cosponsor: 235.72, 205.63, 227.45, 243.53, 250.87 (max 797, 632, 666, 695, 791). Text also states at least 87.85% of House bills had cosponsors in each term (p. 4). Median House passage time 98 days, mean 148 days (p. 11). Roughly 3% of all bills in the ProPublica data were enacted (p. 5). Bills are about 70% of proposed legislation (p. 5).
ext.method: 1) Build monthly undirected weighted cosponsorship tensors: A[t,i,j]pass counts bills introduced in month t that include i and j as sponsor/cosponsors and eventually pass the House; A[t,i,j]tot counts all such bills (p. 6). Edges are symmetric; sponsorship and cosponsorship are treated equally (pp. 5-6). 2) Exponential decay with half-life 6, 12 or 24 months (k = ln(0.5)/half-life), cumulated monthly: C[t,i,j] = sum over n<=t of e^{k(t-n)} A[n,i,j] (Eq. 1-2, pp. 7-8). 3) Party-normalized influence: P[t,i]Dems and P[t,i]Reps are the decayed pass/total ratio summed over co-party members divided by party size (Eq. 3, p. 8). I[t,i] = P_Dems + P_Reps (Eq. 4, p. 8). 4) Bill influence at introduction month t_k: mean or max of I[t_k,i] over cosponsors C_k (Eq. 5, p. 10). 5) Compare passed vs failed bills in non-overlapping 4-month windows via relative difference = (mean passed minus mean failed) / mean failed (pp. 11, 13). Comparators: eigenvector centrality of D = C_pass / C_tot on the largest connected component, eigenproblem D x = lambda x (Eq. 6-7, pp. 15-16); closeness and strength centrality on the same LCC, Appendix A (Eq. 8-9, p. 18). Analysis is descriptive: plots, means and standard errors. No regression, no controls, no formal significance test is reported.
ext.identification: None in the causal sense. The paper makes an associational claim: bill-level influence separates passed from failed bills. No control for bill topic, committee, sponsor or party beyond the party-normalized score construction (the authors list topic and committee as future controls, p. 17). Two features of the construction bear on how the separation should be read. (a) Authors' stated choice (p. 10, lines 417-422): a bill is included in its own influence calculation, so the outcome of the bill being scored can enter its own predictor; authors argue the effect is at most one bill in a large numerator. (b) As written in Sec. 4 (p. 6, 'eventually pass (including possibly in month t)'), A[n] counts a bill as passing whenever it eventually passes, so C[t] can include passage events that happen after month t. The authors do not discuss whether this is look-ahead. This is a reader's reading of the definitions, not a claim the paper makes.
ext.scope: Population: House-originated bills in the 111th-115th Congresses only. Institution: US House of Representatives; Senate, resolutions and enactment are excluded by design (pp. 4-5). Era: January 2009 to January 2019, which the authors tie to rising polarization after 2015 (p. 9, p. 13). Findings are aggregate; the authors explicitly decline to make claims about individual legislators (p. 17).

key_findings.finding: Passed bills have larger bill-level influence than failed bills in every 4-month period from 2009 to 2019, for both mean and max aggregation.
key_findings.numbers: Consistent separation in all 4-month windows; no per-window counts given.

key_findings.finding: Max-cosponsor influence separates passed and failed bills more than mean-cosponsor influence.
key_findings.numbers: Mean relative difference at 6-month half-life: 0.248 (max) vs 0.139 (mean).

key_findings.finding: The max-vs-mean separation holds at longer half-lives.
Half-life choice between 6 and 24 months barely changes discrimination; shorter decay gives slightly larger separation.
key_findings.numbers: Max-influence relative differences 0.248 / 0.223 / 0.203 for 6 / 12 / 24 months; standard errors 0.0139 / 0.0119 / 0.0107.

key_findings.finding: Eigenvector centrality is a much weaker indicator of passage than the influence measure.
key_findings.numbers: Mean relative difference 0.004 (mean eigenvector) and 0.002 (max eigenvector), vs 0.139 and 0.248 for influence.

key_findings.finding: Closeness and strength centrality are also weak indicators, and the authors attribute the failure to dense networks (untested).
key_findings.numbers: Closeness: 0.004 mean, 0.002 max. Strength: 0.004 mean, 0.003 max.

key_findings.finding: Legislator influence scores are small and their distribution mean does not rise over time; the authors hypothesize less collaboration in Congresses 114-115.
key_findings.numbers: Legislator scores range roughly 0 to 0.008. Distribution mean is smallest in Congresses 114 and 115.

key_findings.finding: Bill-level influence declines steeply from about 2015; the authors hypothesize this tracks rising polarization (not tested).
key_findings.numbers: No numeric decline reported in text.

key_findings.finding: Authors' interpretive conclusion: a bill is more likely to pass when one very influential member cosponsors it than when several moderately influential members do. This rests on the max-vs-mean comparison.
key_findings.numbers: Based on the 0.248 (max) vs 0.139 (mean) relative differences at 6-month half-life.

limitations: Authors state the influence notion is simplistic: all legislators are treated identically despite differing external influences and goals (p. 17, lines 650-654).
Results are aggregate only; authors decline to comment on legislator-level rankings because they have more confidence in aggregates (p. 17).
Bill topics, committee assignments and other factors that affect votes are not controlled; authors list this as future work (p. 17).
Influence is symmetric; asymmetric sponsor-to-cosponsor influence is left to future work (p. 7).
Aggregation uses 4-month non-overlapping windows; other windows and overlapping windows are not explored (p. 11).
Only House passage is studied; passage in the originating chamber is the outcome, and enacted-into-law outcomes are not analyzed (pp. 4-5).
Authors call the cosponsorship-derived influence measure 'only a proxy' for legislator influence (p. 17).
Comparison with the legislative-effectiveness score (LES) is not performed (p. 18).
Other network measures (e.g. network efficiency) and polyadic influence are not examined (p. 18).
Explanation for centralities failing (dense networks) is stated as a suspicion, not tested (p. 19).
Authors state no competing interests; funding from UC Presidential Postdoctoral Fellowship (Declarations, p. 22). Code is public at github.com/sarahsotoudeh/LegislativeInfluence (p. 1, p. 22).

by the opinions of others in their social networks during their political decision-making
processes.
An important application of networks in political science is the analysis of how groups of individuals debate, decide, and commit to decisions

takes the reciprocal of this weight to yield a cosponsorship distance between each two legislators, and uses Dijkstra's algorithm to find the shortest distance between each pair of legislators.

Fowler illustrated that such connectedness can help successfully infer the passage of amendments to existing legislation, thereby using properties of bill cosponsorship networks as a proxy for legislator influence.
More than half of the bills that are introduced in the US Congress have at least one cosponsor

. In the 96th Congress (1979-1981), the restriction on the number of cosponsors per bill was removed, allowing cosponsorship to become a more prominent mechanism for Congress members to attempt to garner and express support for bills [30].
. If a bill that they cosponsor does not pass, which is common in Congress, there are no real consequences.
A more nuanced perspective is that cosponsorship ties can indicate the evolving political relationships between members of Congress
may play a role in legislation, even if cosponsor count itself does not give a clear signal of a bill's success

Because support from other people is important in Congress, it seems likely that legislator decision-making is affected by a desire to make or maintain personal relation ships, which may provide social capital for the future.

Draw ing from these ideas, we argue that the passage of a large percentage of bills that a Congress member supports (as demonstrated through cosponsorship) may be an indication that that Congress member is influential
the historical success of their sponsored and cosponsored bills
heir bill sponsorship and cosponsorship relationships with other representatives.
We examine such influence using a bill cosponsorship network in which each representative is a node and an undirected edge exists between representatives i and j if they sponsor or cosponsor a bill.
We suppose that representatives accumulate influence together when the bills that they mutually cosponsor pass.

For both mean cosponsor influence and maximum cosponsor influence, we calculate these relative differences by determining the difference between the mean bill-level influence scores of passed and failed bills and dividing that difference by the mean influence score of failed (trimmed at 40 words; source continues 'bills')
Each point is the mean influence score of bills in the associated 4-month period starting on the date on the horizontal axis
Our computation of influence scores incorporates an exponential decay with a half-life of 6 months
One possibility is to combine contributions of very influential legislators with several moderately influential legislators by employing thresholded means
One can also interpret our legislator influence scores as centrality measures
Eigen vector centrality quantifies the importance of a node based on the importances of its neighboring nodes in a network.
not a strong indicator of bill passage.
The eigenvector centrality of a node is given by its associated entry of the leading eigenvector of the adjacency matrix of a graph
D[t, i, j] = = C[t, i, j]pass C[t, i, j]tot C[t, i, j]tot t s
λ is the leading eigenvalue of D[t]LCC C and x is the associated leading eigenvector
Our computation of eigenvector centralities incorporates an exponential decay with a half-life of 6 months.
Our calculations suggest that our influence notion, which we obtain by analyzing bill cosponsorship relationships through time, is informative about the voting outcomes of bills.

cosponsorship by a single very influential representative appears to be a better indicator of bill-passage success in the US House of Representatives than cosponsorship by several moderately influential representatives.
we treated all legislators identically, but clearly there are many differences between different legislators
For example, it is desirable to account for factors (such as bill topics and committee assignments) beyond legislator influence that affect voting outcomes.
it is worthwhile to examine what major political and/or social events may have influenced the temporal trends that we observed in our influence measure.

However, it differs from our approach by looking at more granular stages of the legislative process, characterizing bills by their importance, and not including a decay factor.

measures: Legislator influence I[t,i] = P_Dems + P_Reps, the decayed ratio of passed to total mutually cosponsored bills, normalized by party size (Eq. 3-4, pp. 8-9). Scores range about 0 to 0.008 (p. 9).
Bill-level influence: mean or max of cosponsors' I[t_k,i] at the introduction month (Eq. 5, p. 10).
Outcome separation: relative difference = (mean bill influence of passed minus failed) / mean of failed, in non-overlapping 4-month windows (p. 11, p. 13).
Exponential decay half-life of 6, 12 or 24 months (pp. 7, 13-14).
Eigenvector centrality on D = C_pass/C_tot, largest connected component (Eq. 6-7, pp. 15-16).
Closeness centrality (Eq. 8) and strength centrality (Eq. 9) on the same LCC, Appendix A (p. 18).

rel.summary_md:
Sotoudeh, Porter and Krishnagopal (arXiv 2406.19554v2) build a pairwise influence score from House cosponsorship covering the 111th to 115th Congresses (2009 to 2019). Each pair's share of jointly cosponsored bills that passed the House is decayed exponentially (half-lives of 6, 12 or 24 months), summed over co-party members and normalized by party size. A bill's influence is then the mean or the max of its cosponsors' scores at introduction. In every non-overlapping 4-month window, passed bills score higher than failed ones. The max-cosponsor score separates them better than the mean (relative difference 0.248 vs 0.139 at a 6-month half-life). Half-life barely matters (0.248 / 0.223 / 0.203). Eigenvector, closeness and strength centralities computed on the same pass/total matrix barely separate passed from failed bills (0.002 to 0.004). The analysis is descriptive only: no controls, no significance tests and no strata. A bill counts toward its own score, and as the formulas are written, edges can include passage that happens after the scoring month.

For Paul's system there are three points. First, the paper is cited as the source of the CU cosponsor network's edge weights, but the built weights depart from it on nearly every parameter: an additive ×3 success multiplier instead of a pass/total ratio, a per-Congress 0.8 decay (half-life of about 6 years), a 1/sqrt(C) size discount, unequal role weights and no party normalization. Second, the centrality result backs retiring direction-blind centrality from the Influence pillar. It also shows that any check of InfluenceScore against bill passage would be circular, because the edges are already weighted by passage. Third, code comments and brain notes cite the paper for claims it never tests, namely recruitment chains and influence versus cosponsor count. Paul's 6-month half-life note is also a mis-transfer: the paper's decay applies to accruing cosponsorship influence, not to stance salience.

bearings.paper_claim: Influence accrues per legislator pair as a decayed RATIO C_pass/C_tot of mutually (co)sponsored bills that eventually pass the House. Sponsor and cosponsor are treated identically, edges are undirected, decay is monthly with half-life 6/12/24 months, scores are normalized by party size (Eq. 1-4), and passage means House passage only. The authors call the result 'only a proxy' (p. 17).
bearings.system_side: The brain records the CU network's edge weights as 'P4 Sotoudeh/Porter/Krishnagopal 2024'. The built rule is w = role(orig 1.0 / regular 0.5; holistic regular 0.2) x SUCCESS_MULT 3.0 if latestAction matches PASSED_RE (origin chamber, both chambers) x 0.8^(congress age) x 1/sqrt(C), summed per directed sponsor->cosponsor pair. This is an additive success boost on raw tie volume, not a pass/total ratio. It has no party normalization, and its decay is per Congress (half-life about 3.1 Congresses, roughly 6 years) rather than monthly. Success is read from the bill's last action at scrape time, so a bill that passed its origin chamber and then stalled can lose the boost (the 2026-08-17 caveat: 2,652 bills, about 14.9% of tie weight).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports only the general idea of weighting ties by joint passage, and only for House bills in 2009-2019 with House passage as the outcome. It provides no evidence for the ×3 multiplier, the 1/sqrt(C) discount, the 2:1 or 5:1 role ratio, the per-Congress decay, Senate ties, or CU-topic bill universes. Every numeric dial is the system's own and has not been validated by this paper. The citation should be read as 'inspired by', not 'implements'.

bearings.paper_claim: Eigenvector centrality on the decayed pass/total matrix (largest connected component) barely separates passed from failed bills: mean relative difference 0.004 (mean) and 0.002 (max), against 0.139 and 0.248 for the influence score. Closeness (0.004 / 0.002) and strength (0.004 / 0.003) are equally weak. The authors suspect network density but did not test it.
bearings.system_side: InfluenceScore = 0.60 weighted out-degree + 0.25 betweenness + 0.15 eigenvector, computed on the success-weighted cosponsor graph. It was retired from Influence% (AB13 = 0) as direction-blind and now feeds only the underdog lens. The component's open question asks whether this centrality predicts passage of the member's sponsored bills.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This backs the retirement only loosely. The paper's centralities are computed on a different matrix (a ratio, undirected, House 2009-2019), and it never tests betweenness or weighted out-degree. Answering the component's open question on the system's graph would also be circular: weighted out-degree sums ties on the member's own sponsored bills, and those ties are already multiplied by 3 when the bill passed. Any passage test needs an as-of network built only from bills resolved before the outcome window.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper measures whether bill-level aggregates of cosponsors' pairwise pass-rate scores separate passed from failed bills. It does not study recruitment, paths, ask success, or per-edge probabilities. It never compares its measure against raw cosponsor count; it only cites prior work that count gives no clear signal (p. 4).
bearings.system_side: The template comment cites the paper ('cosponsorship *influence*, not count, drives passage') as grounding for the max-product 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL recruitment chain'. It describes chain reliability as 'the exact, maximal probability' that the chain holds, applies ASKM = 0.07, and computes chainHold as a product of activeP values.
bearings.transfer_conditions: None. The paper's outcome is passage of the bill, not whether a target joins as cosponsor, and its score is not a probability. The citation overstates what the paper shows, and the 'probability' wording runs into D-025.

bearings.paper_claim: A decayed pass/total success ratio is informative about outcomes. Passed bills carry higher cosponsor pass-ratio influence than failed bills in every 4-month window (relative difference 0.139 mean / 0.248 max at a 6-month half-life). The authors contrast this approach with LES, which has no decay and splits the legislative process into finer stages.
bearings.system_side: The efficiency term is computed per (member, category) as sum(decay x sign x advanced) / sum(decay) over sponsored and original-cosponsored bills. It is a member-level decayed advancement ratio that excludes unknown outcomes, and it is blended with the agenda term before PERCENTRANK.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This gives indirect support only. The paper's ratio is pairwise and aggregated to bills, and it predicts the same bills' passage with the bill's own outcome inside the score. The pillar's ratio is member-level and describes CU-topic advancement. The paper does not show that a member's own success rate measures CU influence or predicts future behaviour. The result is pooled with no strata, so it should be labelled UNSTRATIFIED. It comes from the House in 2009-2019, a period the authors themselves say saw falling influence after 2015.

bearings.paper_claim: Shorter decay gives slightly more separation within the tested range: relative differences of 0.248 / 0.223 / 0.203 at 6 / 12 / 24-month half-lives (SE 0.0139 / 0.0119 / 0.0107). The paper lists a comparison with LES as future work and never runs it.
bearings.system_side: The shadow score applies Volden-Wiseman-style stages with role weights 3/2/1, a 180-day half-life on cosponsor timing, and Congress decay 0.8 to historical terms. That decay is a half-life of about 3.1 Congresses, far longer than the 24-month maximum the paper tested.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper suggests one cheap check: whether a sub-Congress decay changes how well the shadow converges with CEL LES. It cannot set the decay value, because its outcome (separating passed from failed bills) differs from the shadow's goal (convergence with LES). Its half-life evidence also covers only 6-24 months.

bearings.paper_claim: The 6-month half-life is one of three settings for decaying cosponsorship-influence capital, not a stance-salience estimate. Discrimination barely changes between 6 and 24 months (0.248 vs 0.203).
bearings.system_side: The media blend decays each post by 0.5^(age/HL), with HL 2.0 years for press and SOCIAL_HL_YEARS default 0.5 for social.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Not transferable. The paper's decay applies to a different construct (accumulated passage-rate ties) and a different outcome (bill passage). Its flatness across half-lives, if anything, warns against treating any one value as calibrated. The paper does not justify 0.5 years for social posts or 2 years for press.

gaps_exposed: The system has no as-of (time-sliced) network. Success flags come from the latest action at scrape time, so any validation of network measures against passage or advancement uses outcomes from the future. The paper shares a version of this flaw: a bill is included in its own score, and edges count eventual passage.
No outcome-separation check has been run on the system's own success-weighted CU network, comparing mean or max cosponsor strength for advanced and non-advanced CU bills within the same window.

No bill-level aggregation uses the strongest cosponsor (max) rather than an additive or mean signal. The paper's main contrast is max vs mean (0.248 vs 0.139), and none of the cascade, forecaster or path engines has a bill-level max-cosponsor feature.
No party-size normalization on edge weights, and no sensitivity test of decay below one Congress. Both are central parameters in the paper.
Neither the effectiveness shadow nor the network measures have been benchmarked against CEL LES. The paper leaves this open, and Paul highlighted it.
flags: DO NOT RECOMMEND: the paper's eigenvector input D = C_pass / C_tot and its pairwise influence ratio are per-edge volume normalizations. Per-edge volume normalization was measured and REJECTED in this project (association sqrt(Out*In) left Katz ~ volume at +0.552; row-stochastic at +0.477). Adopting the paper's ratio construction would re-propose a rejected design without new evidence.

D-025 conflict: make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:735-738 cites this paper next to wording that calls chain reliability 'the exact, maximal probability' and 'mathematical certainty'. The paper gives no probability, and D-025 bars presenting graph ranks or paths as access or introduction probabilities.

Overclaimed citations: the template comment (:738) and brain note actors/melange-dashboard-june-capstone.md:70 attribute 'influence, not count, drives passage' to the paper. The paper never compares against cosponsor count. The cosponsor-network topic note lists the paper as the source of the edge weights, yet the built formula's ×3 multiplier, 1/sqrt(C), role ratios and per-Congress decay are not in the paper.

The paper's relative differences are pooled across parties and across 2009-2019, with a post-2015 decline the authors attribute to polarization. Any figure quoted from it should carry an UNSTRATIFIED label, along with its window (4-month bins, House 111th-115th) and denominator (mean of failed bills).

Circularity hazard: testing InfluenceScore or weighted out-degree against bill passage on the current graph is contaminated, because edges on passed sponsored bills are multiplied by 3 (congress_member_scraper.R:1925; build_holistic_base.py:73).
Every bearing here is a single-path reading of the paper and the code. It stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's highlight that eigenvector centrality is 'not a strong indicator of bill passage' agrees with the paper (0.002-0.004) and with the system retiring centrality from Influence% (AB13 = 0). Even so, the 0.15 eigenvector share still sits inside InfluenceScore and the underdog lens. His wish for weighted, directed, time-decayed edges is only partly supported. The paper's edges are undirected and treat sponsor and cosponsor identically, so the directed graph (load_network_directed) and the role weighting go beyond the paper. His media-blend note that treats Sotoudeh's 6-month half-life as a decay timescale is a mis-transfer: that decay applies to cosponsorship-influence capital, and the paper shows the choice hardly matters between 6 and 24 months. His LES-contrast highlight is accurate, but the paper never ran the comparison, so it cannot underwrite the effectiveness-shadow design or the pillar weights. His notes are stale on one point: they do not record that the built edge weights depart from the paper on decay scale, ratio vs multiplier, size normalization and party normalization.

related.why: Same senior author (Porter). Committee-network structure is the other half of the House structural picture that this paper's cosponsorship measure omits; the authors list committee assignments as a missing control (p. 17).

Both use House collaboration networks to find effective legislators. Aref & Neal's hidden effective bloc and this paper's 'single very influential cosponsor' finding are both offered against LES-style effectiveness.
Supplies the LES-family effectiveness criterion that this paper explicitly leaves as an untested comparison (p. 18).

Battaglini & Patacchini make Katz-Bonacich centrality the equilibrium target for influence. This paper finds eigenvector, closeness and strength centralities nearly uninformative about passage (0.002-0.004). The outcomes differ (contributions vs passage), so the tension is partial.

Ringe, Victor and Gross also treat network centrality as a measure of legislative influence, using co-voting instead of cosponsorship. Together they show that centrality-as-influence depends on how the network is built.
The dashboard template cites both papers together as grounding for the recruitment chain. Only Chen et al. addresses path reliability; this paper addresses bill-level passage signals.
